So I informed [as interpreted] the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the government and the ministry for national defence that the JNA shouldn't mobilise anyone until these two levels, the state and republican level, reached an agreement. It was my task, because of the women and children, to go and try and find a solution, to return the soldiers to the field, to the factories, et cetera. Because the Bosniak people, the Muslims, didn't want a war. They didn't want to have to kill Serbs and Croats, anyone else, within Yugoslavia or outside the boundaries of Yugoslavia. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] So you intervened with the Muslim members of the brigade and you persuaded them not to take part in this and to return to their homes or to desert, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't on my own. There were six or seven buses. There were women, children, fathers. We had a negotiation team and we asked to speak to representatives. Commander Milosevic was there. He was the commander of the entire garrison in Zaluzani. We discussed the fact that it wasn't possible for the troops to return, et cetera, and my duty [as interpreted] was to prevent this from happening in the territory of Vlasenica municipality. But after the population was warned, the troops did respond. Many of those inhabitants had trust. They believed that it was the former JNA. But when they came to Zaluzani and when they saw who the troops were, there were 7.000 or 8.000 soldiers there, 80 per cent of them were bearded, intoxicated, they had cockades, they were singing nationalist songs, it's an area of about ten kilometres, where there were tanks, Howitzers, other forms of artillery that have been deployed, and when someone sees such things, it is clear that it wasn't possible to find a solution in Bosnia and Herzegovina. All that was possible was for force to be used by a certain party. This is something that was a well-known fact. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] And my very last question concerns your intervention in order to transport the Muslim population and help them to leave Vlasenica. I must admit that I didn't understand what you said very well. Did this just concern the people detained in Susica or did it concern people living in the villages, in the town, who contacted you to intervene to obtain transport for them out of the municipality?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vlasenica, as a town, had already been evacuated. All those who wanted to leave had already left. However, people in the villages believed that they were not guilty of anything, that they were not engaged in any politics, that they were not interested in who was in power, and their sole concern was their own survival. They still remained in their villages. However, the time arrived when the Serb unit entered all these villages. They captured all the men. They evacuated the women and children to Susica. At that moment, Susica was a control point for the women, children, and the elderly. From there, they went to Kladanj. As for the males, they remained in the Susica camp. At that moment, the entire Vlasenica municipality was covered by the Serb units. All the villages were encircled. The women, children, and men were captured. Those who tried to run away were killed immediately. Those who were not killed were brought to Susica, and according to some of their criteria, women, children, and elderly males were transported to Kladanj, and the males were kept in the camp. Most of them never arrived in the free territory of the Federation, and up to this day, nobody knows the whereabouts of these people who remained detained in the Susica camp. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] My question was: Did you receive the calls of the detained people? Did they ask for your intervention? Could they contact you from the detention camp? Could they ask for your intervention once they were detained?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, of course not. They did not have anything to eat or to sleep, let alone having the right to talk to anybody. The detainees had no rights whatsoever. They didn't have the right to food, they didn't have the right to sleep. And people who spent some time there know best how it was. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] But who contacted you, and from Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond where?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were people from Vlasenica who enjoyed some trust. There were people in mixed marriages, Muslims married to Serbs, and there was still a flow of communication. And they feared for the lives of their closest relatives and they intervened, and for as long as I could communicate with Mr. Stanic and Mr. Drakulic, I asked them to help these people get out to the areas in the Federation. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Witness. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Redzic, I also have one question for you. You testified yesterday that Mr. Stanic told you: Muslims will be given Tuzla and Zenica, these two enclaves, that he told you personally: Don't go to Sarajevo. There will be a blood battle there. Did Mr. Stanic tell you where he got his information from that he passed on to you about Tuzla and Zenica and about what would happen in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Realistically speaking, one could not expect him to say where his orders came from, but it is not difficult to assume.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I only asked you whether he told you and whether it would be difficult to guess is a totally different matter. But I do understand your answer correctly that he didn't tell you what was the source of his information.

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we didn't discuss that. This was very late, just before I was about to leave Vlasenica myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, it answers my question. Mr. Redzic, first I'll ask the parties whether there's any need to put additional questions to the witness from the Bench.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Questions put by the Bench.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, just briefly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There will be one or even more questions by Ms. Loukas to be put to you, Mr. Redzic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Redzic, this information in relation to Tuzla and Zenica that you say was conveyed by Mr. Stanic and this question of there being a blood battle in Sarajevo. Of course, these matters are not contained in your statement of 19th of October, 1994, are they?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, that's not a matter that arises out of the questions of the Bench.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, it's clear that they don't, and Your Honours will have the material before you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But I just said that it's not something that came up as a result of the questions of the Bench. It could have been put to the witness in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour seemed uninterested in the contradictions, and I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. I'm not uninterested. I gave you full opportunity to deal with whatever contradiction or even apparent inconsistency. But it's not something that came up as a result of the questions of the Bench.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour. I can just tender the statement, and Your Honour will see that that is new information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any other question you'd like to put?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. But what I could deal with at this stage is the fact that Ms. Cmeric tells me that there are certain issues of translation in relation to some of the questions asked by your brother Judge El Mahdi which I should put on the record now whilst the witness is still here, I feel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: At page 45, line 20, I think what appears in the transcript is "I informed the Presidency." That should be "I was informed by the Presidency."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just try to find it. One second. Yes. Well, at least it's -- you suggested it would be the proper translation, that --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. That's my understanding from Ms. Cmeric, who of course speaks the language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And at page 46, at line 10, the statement was, as in the transcript: "My duty was to prevent." There's a little bit left out there, and that is: "My duty that I was bound to by the Bosnia-Herzegovina Presidency was to prevent."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You say there's a part missing in the translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I just thought I'd deal with those matters I think whilst the witness is still here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is there any -- I don't think there would be any need to seek verification, because otherwise the parties would have to go through the transcripts and see whether the original -- perhaps we could seek confirmation of the correctness. Mr. Redzic, you testified, in response to a question of Judge El Mahdi, that: "Not up until the time that an agreement was reached at the level of the former Yugoslavia and at the level of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that there was no competence for mobilisation." And then your next line was about the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Did you inform them, or were you informed by the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and the government and the ministry for national defence that the JNA shouldn't mobilise anyone? Were you informed by them or did you inform them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina informed all the municipalities that there should be a ban on any further mobilisation until an agreement is reached between Yugoslavia and the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And when mobilisation was carried out illegally, I informed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I stopped you perhaps too early. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just wanted to say that after mobilisation it was my duty to inform the Presidency, the government, and the minister for defence about the situation that had happened and that was in disagreement with the dispatches previously sent from them to us. In a nutshell, this mobilisation was against their orders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you received the information that they shouldn't mobilise, and you reported back that they were mobilising, contrary to the instructions. That's clear. Then the next issue is also a matter of translation. You said it was -- at least, it reads in our transcript that it was your duty to prevent, and our attention has been drawn to the fact that your actual words have been that it was your duty -- that you were bound by the Bosnia-Herzegovina Presidency to prevent, so that it was not just your duty, but you were duty-bound by the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So these matters have been clarified now. Since the witness is still there, Mr. Tieger, is there any -- because we couldn't ask any questions any more once the witness has left. I don't know whether you would have any knowledge about that, but about the transcripts. One is date and the other one was a correction of the -- seems to be a wrong English version of the...

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I don't think that's anything that requires the witness's presence, and in any event, I'm not prepared to address questions that would be of assistance in that regard at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So, therefore, there's no need to deal with that immediately in the presence of the witness. Mr. Redzic, I'd like to thank you very much for having come from far away to The Hague and to have answered questions of both parties and of the Bench. And I wish you a safe trip home again. You are excused.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, and goodbye.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We could deal with the exhibits at this moment, but the Chamber prefers to receive a new version of 259B.1 before giving any decision on the admission into evidence of the exhibits. But we'd rather not let that wait for a couple of months. So, Mr. Tieger, if you would please deal with the matter this afternoon and come back to it tomorrow morning. Then I'd like to ask to the Prosecution whether it is ready to call its next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we are ready to proceed. I should note at this time that the Prosecution -- that this witness will be led by Carolyn Edgerton, who is now at counsel table.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Welcome in the courtroom, Ms. Edgerton. The next witness, there are no protective measures asked for, and your next witness will be Kadira Brkovic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, Madam Usher, may I request you to bring the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, in anticipation of a possible equality of arms argument in light of our new addition to the Prosecution team, I should advise the Court that Mr. Resch, who presented our last witness before we broke for the August recess has left the team and gone back to the United States to work in private practice. So there's no additional gain to the Prosecution team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's not try to compare the number of people involved in Prosecution and Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I must say, I like to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand. It was an understatement, Ms. Loukas. Good morning, Ms. Brkovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: From your answer, I do understand that you hear me in a language you understand. Ms. Brkovic, before giving evidence in this Court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. May I invite you to make that declaration, of which of text will be handed to you now by Madam Usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please be seated. Ms. Brkovic, you will first be examined by counsel for the Prosecution. Ms. Edgerton, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Examined by Ms. Edgerton:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Ms. Brkovic. How are you this morning?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning. Very well, thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ms. Brkovic, before we begin in detail, I'd like to get you to tell us a little bit about yourself, if that's all right. You were born in Plamenice, in Kljuc municipality; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're married and you have three daughters?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've been living in the village of Prhovo in Kljuc municipality since about 1977; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mrs. Brkovic, I'd just like to get you to look at a map that's going to appear on the computer monitor in front of you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And Your Honours, if it could be given a number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you see the map, Mrs. Brkovic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd first like to have the map be given a number.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit number P260.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you see the map, Mrs. Brkovic?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do, but I need to put my glasses on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you bring them with you today?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you identify the village of Prhovo on that map, Mrs. Brkovic?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how far do you see the village of Prhovo to be from the town of Kljuc?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I might just interrupt at this point. I think that the witness is a little bit too close to the microphones, which will create problems with the translation and the hearing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I heard that there was some technical problem. You don't have to worry that much about speaking into the microphone, Ms. Brkovic. It's just if you speak that one or both of the microphones will catch your words anyhow.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm thinking perhaps it might be more useful for the witness to actually have the map in front of her rather than sort of going up to the screen --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. There are two ways of doing that. First of all, to give the witness a copy of the map, a hard copy. And the other way of doing it could also be to enlarge a bit the picture on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Brkovic, how far is the village of Prhovo from the town of Kljuc?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: Ten kilometres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is there a road link between the two places?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you give us an idea of how big your village is? How many houses, perhaps, are located in your village?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: 45, I believe, thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that the case in 1992?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In 1992, at the moment, there are not as many. They have been destroyed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in 1992, do you have an idea of approximately how many people were living in each house?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: In every house, there were four or five or even more family members.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the village of Prhovo itself, is that a Muslim village or a Serb village?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: In the middle, it was Muslim, and around this centre, there were Serbian suburbs, also called Prhovo. Those were Serbian houses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, as I said earlier, the time we're going to talk about is late May of 1992. At that time, is it correct that you were alone in the village with your three daughters?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I was alone at home, but there were other people in the village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where was your husband at that time?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: My husband was in Germany at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if we can go to approximately one week before the attack on your village. Do you recall anything unusual happening at that time?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: I remember two neighbours of mine came and told me that they saw the army by Nikola Popovic's house, and then a lorry drove through the village of Prhovo, towards Peci.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where does Nikola Popovic live, or where did he live at that time?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: He lived in his house, a kilometre and a half from the village of Prhovo itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you tell the Court which direction Peci is in relation to Prhovo village. Perhaps I can assist by saying: Is it north, south, east, or west?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: I can show it on the map.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps we can have the -- it might be best to put the map on the ELMO, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we could do so. Well, of course it's on our screen anyhow, but is the direction of any specific interest? Because, of course, the Court sees where Peci is in relation to -- so unless there is any specific relevance for asking the witness whether it was north or west, we see where it is on the map.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That's fine, then, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mrs. Brkovic, you mentioned a lorry driving through the town.

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: The village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have occasion after that to see any soldiers coming through the town, the village?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: I saw them in the lorry. I saw them wearing uniforms, carrying arms, and I remember it was a Saturday when this lorry drove through.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Mrs. Brkovic, can we move forward in time to one week later. Could you tell us what happened then.

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: A week later, we saw a fire and smoke in Plamenice. A few shells exploded some 500 metres away from us. Those were either shells or some sort of a loud explosion. We were in our houses until the soldiers came. They asked us to surrender weapons. I didn't have any weapons to surrender. I was in my house with my daughters. And I heard somebody saying: "Surrender. We won't do anything to you." And one neighbour was shouting: "Get out of your houses. They are setting houses on fire." We didn't know which houses would be set on fire, so I left my house. They started gathering us in one place, and they said they wouldn't do anything to us, for us to gather in that one place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Brkovic, if I could just stop you for a second and go back over some of the things that you've talked about. It sounds like there's many things happening at the same time. Could you make it clear to the Court what did you first notice going on?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: First we noticed people gathering, and when this guy said that houses were being set on fire, we first wanted to hide in a cellar. And then they started shooting after us, and then we started walking towards a little forest. The women and the children. There were some 15 of us altogether.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Brkovic, where were your daughters at that time?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: My daughters were with me, the three daughters of mine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you and your three daughters went to the forest; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: No. The first evening when things happened, when we started walking, it was on a Sunday. Actually, it was a Saturday, Saturday Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond evening. I can't remember the date. And then my two daughters, with my brother-in-law and his wife, went to the forest. The third daughter, who has weak legs, was afraid to go. She couldn't go. I tried to convince her to go, because the other two had already hid in the forest. When we arrived there, some six or seven of us altogether, there were people shooting after us, shooting at our backs. We were quiet. Some of us cried. The two daughters were not with me. The third daughter was with me. A neighbour of ours went to a Serbian village to inquire what would happen to us, what were they doing to us. And when he arrived there, they told him: "You shouldn't hide in the forest. You should go back home." Two guys of Serbian ethnic origin arrived with him, and when we saw them, we left the forest. We thought they would kill us anyway. So we went to a little meadow. We saw that they were armed. They told us: "Go to your homes. We won't do anything to you." We believed them. We spent the night in Fehret Hadzic's house with my two daughters. There was some other women there as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I stop you there, Mrs. Brkovic. So you were in the forest for some time. You went out of the forest after some Serbs from a neighbouring settlement had assured you it was okay to go back to your homes; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They said we would be safe in our houses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you got back to your village, what did you see?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: It was night when we returned that night. It was dark.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I need you to perhaps slow down a little bit so that we can go through each thing step by step, if that's okay. Now --

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: When we returned, we saw a house on fire, and that was on the following day, when they beat a few people to death. That was on a Saturday. There were some people with swollen heads. Their backs were red. And the others were covered in blood, with injuries on their heads. They had beaten up five or six people, and they had set a house on fire. We stayed there. We extinguished the fire, and this is where we stayed to spend the night there. And then there was Sunday. On that day --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Brkovic, if we can just stop you again. So we've gone quickly through two days at the end of May, haven't we?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Brkovic, may I ask you the following: I fully understand that you want to tell your story. It is important for this Chamber to sometimes hear a bit more details about one aspect, a little bit less details on other aspects. Would you carefully listen to the question and try to focus your answer on the specific question that has been put to you. So when you testified that you arrived back in your village at night, I would expect Ms. Edgerton to ask you what you would see the next morning. Then tell us what you saw the next morning. But if she asks you what you did the next morning, tell us that you got up and stayed in the house or went out of the house. So try very much to concentrate on the specific questions put to you by Ms. Edgerton, although I fully understand that you would like nothing else than to just tell whatever happened to you. But then we might miss some details. So if you could try to concentrate carefully on the specific questions. Yes? Please proceed, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Brkovic, now --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Brkovic, on this second day, you've said you went to the forest again and saw a burning house when you came out. Can you tell us why you went to the forest again?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, they were setting fire to houses. That's when we went to the forest. We went to the shelter, to take shelter there. They shot after us. And that's when we went to the forest.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mrs. Brkovic, is this the first day or the second day?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: That was the second time. I didn't say that correctly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So on the second day, who were you in the forest with?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: I was with my daughters. There was one of my daughters there. In fact, two daughters, with my brother-in-law, and the sister-in-law. One of them was with me. That was the evening on which they were cleaning the forest. That was the first day. That was the first time we went to the forest.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Brkovic, the first time you went to the forest, you were with your daughters and your brother-in-law and his family; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: The first time, yes. My brother-in-law didn't go the first day. The first day was when they came to take the weapons and when they wanted to set fire to the houses, when they started shooting at us, that's when I went to the forest.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Brkovic, you say on the first day they came to take the weapons. Can you tell us now who came to take the weapons.

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't see them, because I didn't even go to the village. There were a lot of them. There were vehicles. That's what we heard when we were in the forest. They would just pass by. But I don't know how many of them there were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So how do you know, then, that they came to take the weapons, Mrs. Brkovic?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: I know that they called out over a megaphone and asked us to hand over the weapons. They said that they wouldn't do anything to us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Once you heard that announcement over the megaphone, did you or your family do anything?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: We then went out of the house. We were thinking of going there when we heard the shooting. That's when we went to the forest. We set off in the direction of the shelter. They fired at us, and we then set off in the direction of the forest.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You stayed in the forest, then, for some time that first day; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: [Inaudible]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the second day you went to the forest again. Do you remember why you went to the forest the second day?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: The second day we went to the forest and they said that they were cleaning the forest. There was ethnic cleansing. They were cleansing the forest. We heard shooting. That's why we went.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, Mrs. Brkovic, you heard shooting. You went with your family to the forest. And now you've mentioned they were cleaning the forest. When you say they were cleaning the forest, what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: They used the term "ethnic cleansing" on the radio. We didn't know what it meant. They didn't want anyone to remain in the forest. They were afraid, or something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "they," Mrs. Brkovic, who do you mean?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I mean they were neighbours of ours there, and they told us everything. On the whole, of Serbian nationality, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, do you remember how long you stayed in the forest the second day?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. Night was falling. But I couldn't tell you what time it was exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned cleaning the forest. While you were in the forest that second day, did you hear or see anything unusual?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, they were passing through the forest and shooting. I think they were lined up every three to five metres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, again, when you say "they," who do you mean? What did you see?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: We didn't see anything at the time. We only heard the shooting. A neighbour went to ask the Serbs, to ask them what we should do, to see whether they would guarantee we could stay there and that there wouldn't be any problems. They said: "Can't you see that it's not safe in the forest? Go home." We believed them and arrived with two other Serbs. They called out to other people who were hiding, to women and children, and told them to go home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who were these two other Serbs?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: Marinko Suknovic and Stojan Tekic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you know them?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: They were neighbours of ours. They lived perhaps a kilometre away from us. Marinko Suknovic did. I had a shop. They would go there. So I knew all of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So I take it from what you're saying, you saw Marinko Suknovic and Stojan Tekic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How were they dressed?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: He had a uniform. He had an automatic rifle. Marinko had some sort of work overalls. He had some kind of a weapon. I don't know what kind of a weapon. I know they took something from Sefik Medanovic. He took that weapon on the second day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So after being told this by these two Serbs, did you then return to your village?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: We did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see anything when you got there?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: We spent the night at home. We didn't see anything that night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mrs. Brkovic, you've mentioned a burning house. Could you place that incident in time for us?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: It was on a Saturday. The last Saturday in May. I don't know the date, though.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you think it was the first day or the second day or a day following that?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: It was the day after, when the house was set on fire. On Saturday, they beat those people up, and the house was on fire. On Sunday, we spent the night in the house that burnt down. One floor had burnt down. That's where we spent the night. On Monday, that's when they killed everyone and that's the night that we spent there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the day that they burnt the house and the day that they beat people were the same day; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: Those were two days. I couldn't tell you exactly. Yes, when they set fire to the house, they beat the people. It was on the same day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see people with marks of beating on them, Mrs. Brkovic?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know any of those people?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: I do. Camil Medanovic, I know Teufik Medanovic, Sefik Medanovic, Ekrem Hadzic, Tehvid Osmanovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe some of the marks of beating that you saw?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: On Camil, I could see that his head was swollen. He had bandaged it. It hurt a lot. His back had been torn. There was a cross made on his back. He said he couldn't even say how much his head hurt. It was terrible to see him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember where you spent that --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember where you spent that night, Mrs. Brkovic?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where was that?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: It was in Fehret Hadzic's house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you and your family alone in that house?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: No, we weren't. There were other women there and children. There were a lot of us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened the next day? Can you tell us about that, then? What unusual -- what was the first unusual thing that you saw happen?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: Monday -- on Sunday -- that was the next day. That was a Monday. We then saw the troops arriving. We didn't think they would do anything to us. Naturally, we were in front of our houses as they arrived in the village. We saw a personnel carrier arriving. The women and children took shelter in a shelter. There were a lot of them there, and it wasn't possible to fit any other people in there. My brother-in-law said: "Why are you going to hide? They won't do anything to you." We sat down at a table at my brother-in-law's house when they arrived in the village. They started calling people out. They said: "Come here. We won't do anything to you." When we approached them, they started swearing at us, took us to a house, to Karanfil Osmanovic's house, and lined us up there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Brkovic, if I can stop you there, and again we can go back to the beginning of your story for that day. You said you saw troops arriving.

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall -- do you have any idea how many there were?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: There were a lot of them. I think there were about 2.000 of them. They were so numerous that it was impossible to count them. Some of them arrived in buses. They went around the villages and through the forest. Some arrived in the village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, who were these troops?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: They were all dressed. Some of them had stockings on them. Some had camouflage on them. There were all sorts of troops there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were any of them in uniform?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of uniform?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: There were camouflage uniforms, there were some green uniforms, and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned that they called people to come out; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember how they called people to come out?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: They said: "Come here. We won't do anything to you. Surrender." Everyone headed towards them. We had to. We didn't know what to do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, Mrs. Brkovic, when you say "everyone," let's talk about the people you were with at that time. Who in your family went towards them?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: My three daughters, myself, my brother-in-law, his wife, the daughter, two daughters, in fact, the son. There were quite a few other neighbours who were in the vicinity. We all set off in that direction. Safet Medanovic was with us, Suvad Hadzic. We were sitting together and we all set off in that direction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is your brother-in-law's name, Mrs. Brkovic?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: Ilfad Brkovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now you said they took you to the front of Karanfil Osmanovic's house; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At this point I'd like to show you another photograph, if I may. If it could receive a number, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And I think you'll be able to see it on the screen shortly.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P261.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, if you would be able to find somewhere in the next five minutes a moment for the next break.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, keeping in mind the evidence to come, perhaps we can have the witness's comments about this photograph and then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I leave it up to you, but just to find a moment somewhere in the next five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you should -- Your Honour should have the photo on your screen, and Mrs. Brkovic has the -- I'm sorry. That's not the correct photograph. This one, 02033317. There we go. Now everyone has the same photograph available to them. Mrs. Brkovic, do you recognise the house that you see in the picture in front of you?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us what that is.

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: I can. That was Sefik Medanovic's shop. We were lined up across the road against the wall by a house there. It's 20 or 30 metres from the road. They lined up all the people, the women, and behind them, the children.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, Mrs. Brkovic, you were lined up across the road from this house, against the house of Karanfil Osmanovic?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, just again, if you can tell me: You say, "They lined us up." When you say "they," who are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about the Serbian troops.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know the ethnicity of these troops?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: I know that there were no other armed forces there, apart from them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps this would be a suitable time for a break, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it is. We'll have a break until 10 minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mrs. Brkovic, if we can just go back to the events we were talking about before the break. If I understand it correctly, you, your three daughters, your brother-in-law, his wife, and their two daughters and son, all gathered at the Karanfil Osmanovic house; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in front of the house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your brother-in-law's name is Ilfad and your sister-in-law, what was her name?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: Asima.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the names of their children?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: Nisveta, Elvedin, Zehra. Those were their names.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you were describing before the break how you were lined up. You said: They lined up all the people, women and children behind. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, could you be perhaps a little bit more precise? How were the people lined up in relation to the Osmanovic house?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They were next to the wall. They all faced the wall. First, men, women, then children. They were all lined along the wall with their hands up, and they were not supposed to look. Their eyes had to be covered.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you remember who ordered that they weren't supposed to look and their hands should be up?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly who it was. Somebody from that group said that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall hearing such an order given?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They were all shouting: "Hands up." And that's what was done.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So people were standing facing the wall. And where exactly were their hands?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: I can show you. Like this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So your hands were clasped behind your head; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened once you were lined up?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: They singled out a woman and also to call people from the wood and tell them that if they didn't leave the forest, that they were the Green Berets, and if they didn't leave the forest, they would all be killed, even the baby that was there. This guy was telling her what she was supposed to repeat after him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember the name of the woman?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: Sadeta Medanovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned the word "Green Berets." To your knowledge, were there any Green Berets operational in the area at that time?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: No. I was not aware of that. I didn't know anything of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did something happen after that?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: One guy said: "Our commander is impatient. Take out five people to be shot." And they called the names of Hasan Medanovic, Braco Medanovic. We told them that they were not there, that they were in Germany, and then they started cursing our Ustasha mother, they started telling us that we were lying. And then they pointed their fingers at other men that would be taken out of the line. They were all taken out of the line. Shall I tell you their names?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. But if I can just, before you do that, go back a bit. These people called out two men by name; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they call out any other men by name after that?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They were picking people out of the line?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in front of us, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you were able to, from your post, still see who they picked out of the line?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They were standing right in front of me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who were they?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: Isak Mesic, Halil Medanovic, Izet Hadzic, Hasim Hadzic, and Safet Medanovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did something happen to these men?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: They said that they would be shot. Then we heard shots and then we were told that they would rest in peace, and we assumed that they were dead. And then they picked out Sefik Medanovic. He was beaten with all sorts of things, whatever they had handy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you say "they picked out Sefik Medanovic," who picked out Sefik Medanovic?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't see who picked him. I only recognised Dane Popovic. I recognised his voice, shouting at him. He was cursing his mother. He told him that he was a fucking politician. I saw that there were six of them beating him. They threw him on the ground and he was crying and wailing. He was behind my back, so I could hear his cries clearly. He was beaten to death, without a single bullet being fired.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, how did you know the voice of one Dane Popovic, and who was he?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: He was a neighbour of mine. He lived between Plamenice and Prhovo, and I was rather familiar with his voice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did you have occasion later, then, to see the body of Sefik Medanovic?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you have occasion to later see the bodies of those five men who you spoke about earlier?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I saw all of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, could you tell us what happened -- what you saw and heard happen, then, after Sefik Medanovic was beaten.

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: First I saw my brother-in-law's daughter dying in her mother's arms. I suppose that a stray bullet hit her in the forehead. I saw this child dying in her mother's arms. That was the first victim I saw dying. And later on they told us that they were taking people away one by one. And they told us not to leave that place until they left. Sefik Medanovic's mother went there. They started loading people onto a lorry. They threw away their documents. And some of them were on foot, walking towards Peci. When Sefik Medanovic's mother saw his son dead, she said: "Kill me too." But they didn't wait. They fired a burst of fire, some three metres away from me. So the second group of troops that came through the forest also arrived. They cursed us. They had arms and ammunition. And they walked and they carried all this ammo. There was a lot of ammunition.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mrs. Brkovic, you've talked about a very large number of things there in those few seconds, and I'd like to stop you right there and go back to where you began. Because I think it's important for everyone to understand the sequence of events here as best you remember them. Now, you've mentioned several things here. You've mentioned Sefik Medanovic's mother seeing her son dead and asking to be killed. And then a burst of gunfire. But what you first mentioned was your brother-in-law's daughter dying in her mother's arms. Could you maybe think about that and see if you've given us the right chronological sequence of events.

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. First I saw her dying and then they opened fire again. Then Fatima Medanovic asked to be killed. Both her and her daughter-in-law. And then again fire was opened, a burst of fire, a burst of gunfire was opened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you tell me, then, what happened to the people who were standing, I suppose, in front of you in the line, who were facing the wall of the Osmanovic house?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: I've already said, they were loaded onto a lorry. Some of them were forced to walk away from there. They cursed us, told us not to move before they came back. Then a second group of troops arrived, and they were passing through.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were these people who were in front of you taken in and loaded onto the lorry before the burst of gunfire or after?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: First, they were shot at, and then, when those men were taken away, they shot at the women.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where was your brother-in-law? Did you see?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: I saw him taken away in front of me, and he was either forced to walk towards Peci village or was loaded onto a lorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, what happened to you as a result of that burst of gunfire?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: When the men were taken away, they started shooting. A bullet hit me. I was still conscious. I was still standing on my feet. My daughter had left the line and hid under a staircase. My older daughter and my brother-in-law's daughter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what about your two younger daughters? Where were they?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: My younger daughters were in front of me. They were on the ground, lying on the ground in front of me when fire was opened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how -- you mentioned that you were wounded. Can you tell us how you realised that?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: I felt that it was hot. I was burnt. And then I was wounded again, and then this was it. I realised I was wounded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How were you wounded a second time?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: When the men were taken away, they said: "There is nothing for us to do here. Throw something, a Zolja or a grenade." And this happened from then on, I don't remember anything. All of a sudden it was all dark around me. Those of us in the middle survived and the ones in front of the line all died. I lost consciousness. I felt like I had been given anaesthesia, you know. I was totally, completely lost.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you eventually -- you eventually regained consciousness. What did you see around you?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: I heard people crying. I saw my daughter and I heard her saying: "Our mother is dead." And the other daughter said: "Just lie still. Let her be." Then I touched myself. I touched my back. I could feel that I was wounded, that I was seriously wounded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you then do?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: I told my daughters to go to a cellar, to Karanfil Medanovic's [as interpreted] house. Round a wall there was a cellar. We crawled to that cellar. I took a headscarf from a woman, and I dressed my wounds so as to prevent blood loss.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if I can just pause you at this moment to show you another photograph with the ERN number 02033316. It should also be on the screen in front of you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number P262.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recognise the house in this picture, Mrs. Brkovic?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is it?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: This is the house in front of which we were lined up for execution.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you mentioned that once you regained consciousness, you and your daughters went to the basement of Karanfil Osmanovic's house. Do you see that house in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it. You can see the basement as well. It's all there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that's the basement of the building on the left-hand side of the photograph; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in the basement, in the cellar of this house, once you had found your wounds, what did you then do?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: I heard people crying very loud. I could see that my older daughter was not there. I thought that she was dead. So I went out to look for her.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened then?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: The wounded people cried loud. They asked for water. I gave them water to drink.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You found your daughter?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: Then my daughter came from where she had been hiding under the staircase, together with my brother-in-law's daughter. She asked me: "Mom, are you alive?" I said: "Yes."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What then did you do?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: We stayed there a little while. It was already night. Otherwise, they would have searched every house and none of us would have stayed alive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about some of the other wounded? Did anyone make any effort to help them?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We placed them in Sulejman Medanovic's house. There were four persons seriously wounded. Three of them couldn't walk, and my brother-in-law's wife could walk, so she walked there on her own.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who were the other women?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: Hava Medanovic was one, Enesa Medanovic, and Rubija Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To your knowledge, did all four of those women survive the night?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: Two did, two didn't. Two were dead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was that?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: Rubija was dead, and Hava was dead, Hava Hadzic [as interpreted]. Hava Medanovic and Rubija Hadzic were dead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how do you know that?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: In the morning we saw that they were dead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see the two other women alive the next morning?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you do the next morning?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: The next morning we started walking to Humici village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you have occasion after that to go back to your own village?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Three days later, on the fourth day, maybe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us about that visit?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: We went to see what had happened to the people who stayed behind. We saw two skeletons by the door. The house was burning down and you couldn't see much of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. What house was burning down?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: Sulejman Medanovic's house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see the two wounded women who were still alive when you left Prhovo again?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: No. We just found bones, skeletons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who did you think those skeletons belonged to?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: We knew that only four of them were there. Two we found exactly in the place where we left them, and the other two were by the door.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you think anything as a result of finding them by the door?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: We knew that they had burnt down. We didn't know what else to think. They probably wanted to save themselves from the fire. They wanted to leave. But they couldn't muster the strength.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you receive any information that made you think they were alive at the time the fire had been set?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. A neighbour of mine also stayed there that night, one day after us, and in the morning she heard voices. She went to see them and she took them some coffee, and they could still be saved at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I take it that you left Prhovo after this visit and returned to Humici; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: About how far is Humici from Prhovo?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: Six kilometres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you made this journey on foot?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you next go to Prhovo after this?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: On the ninth day after that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us how that came about and what led up to it?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: We wanted to bury our members of family. We wanted to collect their bodies. We wanted to return to our homes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So who did you have to ask to be able to return to your homes?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: We went to the Serbian command to ask them if we could collect those bodies that were already worm-infested and rotting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did the Serbian command say?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: They simply wouldn't allow us to do that. Every day a man would go there to ask. And on the ninth day, he told them that we would all be poisoned with all that, and on the ninth day, finally they allowed us to go up there and collect the bodies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you saying that he told them "we would all be poisoned," I don't quite understand. How would that happen?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. It was terrible at the time. There were flies transmitting this. It smelled very bad.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did this man who received permission tell you what the Serb command told him?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He said we should go there and collect the victims by 11.00 or they would come to bury them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how many people went to collect those victims?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps about 15 of us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were one of these volunteers?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did you do when you got to the village?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: The men collected the dead. We went home to get a little food. We went to our homes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know how many bodies were collected that day?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, 38.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did that include victims from the location at which you were wounded?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. On the whole, it was from that location.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did that include any children, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were children, the youngest of whom was 6 or 7. There were 10-year-old children too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any family members among those bodies you located that day?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was that?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: I saw my brother-in-law's wife, his daughter, and there were other neighbours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did -- that day, were the group of you able to locate any of the men who had been taken away?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: No. But a bit further down below, they found seven or eight of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: At this point I'd like to show you, Mrs. Brkovic, another photograph. The number, ERN number, 02033315.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number P263.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Looking at that photograph before you, Mrs. Brkovic, do you recognise that location?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's where the bodies were buried.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at the top of the photograph, you see two houses, one on the right and a kind of ruin on the left-hand side. What are those houses?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whose houses are they?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: Karanfil Osmanovic and Sefik Medanovic's houses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say they found a number of the men who had been taken away at that location, did you have any family members who were recovered at that location?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: No. On the whole, they were neighbours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at this juncture, I'd like to show you one document, bearing the ERN number 00473294. That's the ERN number of the B/C/S copy.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number P264.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps I could just give you a few minutes to have a look at that document, Mrs. Brkovic, and read the names that are listed out on that document to yourself. Mrs. Brkovic, if I can take you in particular to the bottom of the page and the list of names that appears there. I see Sefik Medanovic, Teufik Medanovic, Safet Medanovic, Alaf [phoen] Medanovic, Izet Hadzic, Hasim Hadzic, Ilfad Brkovic, and Isak Mesic. Do you know these people?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was the last time you saw them alive?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: The last time I saw them was in the line-up with me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you see at the bottom of the page, before the list of names begins, there's a reference that says "Note: In fighting with army and police members, in addition to the above named who were captured in the zone of combat operations and imprisoned, the following persons were killed." Now, to your knowledge, were any of these men involved in fighting at the time you saw them or the period leading up to that?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: No. No resistance was mounted of any kind. Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To your knowledge, were any of these men Green Berets?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To your knowledge, on the day you last saw them alive, were any of these men in possession of any weapons?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, going back to the burial of the bodies you and the group of people recovered from Prhovo, can you tell me how they were ultimately buried?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: An excavator came to bury them. The man who asked for them to be excavated, he said: "If the excavator doesn't leave, you will be buried alive here."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who brought the excavator?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't. I don't know the people. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you recognise any of the people who were there operating the excavator?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, on that occasion when you were back in your village to bury the dead, did you go back to your own house at all?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did you do there?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: I took some things for the children and some food that I had in the house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Anything else?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: Nothing else. They didn't let us do anything else until they had finished their work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to remain in your village and go back to your house?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: Everything had been burnt down. One of the rooms had burnt down. Everything else was black. There was no electricity. Nothing remained there, none of the utilities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where, then, did you go?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: We then returned to the Humici village again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how long did you remain there?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: For three months.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you have to do anything to be able to leave there?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: In Humici, you mean to move on from Humici?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was that?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: We had to request to visit someone, to stay with someone. We didn't have anything to eat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you ultimately travel -- how were you ultimately able to travel out of the village of Humici, to leave?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: We had to hand over our property. We had to de-registered and say that we were moving out permanently.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you do that?

utterances.speaker: KADIRA BRKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we went to the municipal building. We signed a document saying what we were leaving. We de-registered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, may I ask you a question. But perhaps I'll first ask the witness: Do you understand or speak any English?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Would you please take off your headphones for one second. Ms. Edgerton, how much time would you still need? Because looking at the statements the witness has given, it seems to the Chamber that you're close to a finalisation. For perhaps obvious psychological reasons, the Chamber would like the cross-examination to start, if it were only for a couple of minutes. I hope that the parties do understand what makes it -- so therefore, since we usually sit until a quarter to 2.00, and I'm looking at the interpreters whether we could, well, perhaps have five or seven or eight minutes more, if you would conclude and if there would be a possibility to start with the cross-examination for a couple of minutes, that would, in the view of the Chamber --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think that the parties will understand for the well-being of the witness later this day up until tomorrow in the afternoon, it might be good that we -- that she has answered the first questions in cross-examination. So, therefore, if you would keep that in mind, and to the extent possible, finish as quickly as possible. Because this courtroom is needed after half an hour break.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In fact, Your Honour, I was about to thank Mrs. Brkovic, because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please do so. Yes, put your...

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mrs. Brkovic, I wanted to thank you now for being here today, because that concludes the questions I have to ask you now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Ms. Edgerton. Could I ask the witness again to take her earphones off for just one second. Ms. Loukas, we are now about to start the cross-examination, as I explained. Just for your information, as I told the parties yesterday, the Chamber has at its disposal the statements in order to be better able to control the examination of the witnesses. The Chamber noted that there are quite some differences in the various statements the witness has given. The Chamber also noticed that there are elements in those statements that are similar or even exactly the same. So we both have seen the similarities and the differences. You also are aware that under the Statute and the Rules, this Chamber has to pay specific attention to those that were victimised by the conflict, and there are some good reasons to believe that the present witness may be in the category of victims.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can I think assist in this regard. I don't actually have any cross-examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No cross-examination at all. Well, of course, it's the first time. So I don't have to give you any further guidance.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I don't think you have to go any further, and I don't think we have to waste any more court time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Thank you very much for this information, Ms. Loukas. Mrs. Brkovic, it certainly is explained to you by Ms. Edgerton or by counsel for the Prosecution that usually after you've answered the questions put to you by the Prosecution, that then questions will be put to you by the Defence. I just was informed by the Defence that they have no further questions for you, and the other Judges informed me that they have no further questions for you, and I also have no further questions for you. That means that where you might have expected to have to answer questions of the Defence and of the Bench as well, that by answering the questions of the Prosecution, that your examination is now already concluded. I'd like to thank you very much for coming, answering questions put to you. The Chamber is aware that it might not have been easy for you, because your answers indicated clearly that these were traumatic events for you on which you had to testify. The Chamber highly appreciates that you have come and that you testified, and we wish you a safe trip home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Usher, you may escort Ms. Brkovic out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will adjourn now and we'll resume tomorrow -- yes, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I mention one matter regarding scheduling tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We have a witness from Vlasenica scheduled tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand that we're going to try to proceed by Rule 89(F).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: There's a possibility then, depending on the amount of cross-examination that we might finish with him tomorrow, before the end of the day. The next witness will probably not be ready until Thursday morning. So if we could do some housekeeping matters or maybe some Rule 92 bis read-ins.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I would like to suggest that, if it occurs that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I was telling your programme, I saw it again and again to read into the transcript some material. We will adjourn until tomorrow at 2.15 p.m., in Courtroom III, this same courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 1st day of September, 2004, at 2.15 p.m. 17 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
